title: Newfoundland and Labrador
wiki_lead:
Newfoundland and Labrador is the easternmost province of Canada, in the country's Atlantic region. It comprises the island of Newfoundland and the continental region of Labrador, with an area of 405,212 km2 (156,453 sq mi) and a population of 552,462 in 2026. Newfoundland with its neighbouring islands has 94% of the province's population, with more than half in the Avalon Peninsula. Labrador has a land border with the province of Quebec and a short border with Nunavut on Killiniq Island. The French overseas collectivity of Saint Pierre and Miquelon lies about 20 km (12 mi) west of the Burin Peninsula.
In 2021, 99.4% of residents reported English as their native language, making Newfoundland and Labrador Canada's most linguistically homogeneous province. Much of the population is descended from English and Irish settlers, with the majority immigrating from the early 17th century to the late 19th century.
St. John's, the capital and largest city, is Canada's 22nd-largest census metropolitan area and home to about 40% of the province's population. St. John's is the seat of the provincial House of Assembly and its highest court, the Court of Appeal.
Until 1949, the Dominion of Newfoundland was a separate dominion in the British Empire. In 1933, the House of Assembly of the self-governing dominion voted to dissolve itself and to hand over administration of Newfoundland and Labrador to the British-appointed Commission of Government. This followed the suffering caused by the Great Depression and Newfoundland's participation in the First World War. On March 31, 1949, it became the tenth and most recent province to join the Canadian Confederation as "Newfoundland". On December 6, 2001, the Constitution of Canada was amended to change the province's name from "Newfoundland" to "Newfoundland and Labrador".

Names
In 1499 King Henry VII in a letter referred to the newly encountered landmass explored in 1497 by Sebastian and John Cabot as "new founde land." In Portuguese, it is Terra Nova (while the province's full name in that language is Terra Nova e Labrador), which literally means "new land" and is also the French name for the province's island region (Terre-Neuve). The name "Terra Nova" is in wide use on the island (e.g. Terra Nova National Park). The influence of early Portuguese exploration is also reflected in the name of Labrador, which derives from the surname of the Portuguese navigator João Fernandes Lavrador.
Labrador's name in the Inuttitut/Inuktitut language (spoken in Nunatsiavut) is Nunatsuak (ᓄᓇᑦᓱᐊᒃ), meaning "the big land" (a common English nickname for Labrador). Newfoundland's Inuttitut/Inuktitut name is Ikkarumikluak (ᐃᒃᑲᕈᒥᒃᓗᐊᒃ), meaning "place of many shoals". Newfoundland and Labrador's Inuttitut / Inuktitut name is Ikkarumikluak aamma Nunatsuak.

grok_lead: Newfoundland and Labrador is Canada's easternmost province, consisting of the island of Newfoundland situated in the Gulf of St. Lawrence and the continental Labrador territory on the North American mainland, divided by the Strait of Belle Isle. The province spans approximately 405,000 square kilometers, featuring a rugged Atlantic coastline, dense boreal forests in Labrador, and a subarctic to humid continental climate influenced by the Labrador Current and Gulf Stream. With a population of 549,911 as of July 1, 2025, it is one of Canada's least populous provinces, concentrated primarily on the Avalon Peninsula of Newfoundland, where the capital and largest city, St. John's, resides. Formerly a self-governing dominion until financial strains from the Great Depression prompted suspension of responsible government in 1934, Newfoundland and Labrador entered Canadian Confederation on March 31, 1949, following referenda that narrowly favored union over renewed independence or continued British commission rule. The province's economy, with a nominal GDP of $40.7 billion in 2022, has transitioned from reliance on the cod fisheryâdevastated by the 1992 moratorium due to stock collapseâto diversification in offshore petroleum extraction, mining (including nickel and iron ore), hydroelectricity from Labrador's rivers, and emerging aquaculture. This shift, bolstered by developments like the Hibernia oil field and Voisey's Bay mine, has mitigated earlier post-Confederation fiscal dependencies, though per capita debt remains elevated amid debates over resource revenue allocation and federal equalization payments. Historically marked by early Norse exploration around 1000 CE and sustained European fishing outposts from the 16th century, the region contends with legacies of Indigenous displacement, including the extinction of the Beothuk people by the early 19th century amid colonial expansion and resource competition. Today, it balances cultural distinctivenessâevident in dialects, music, and festivalsâwith modern challenges like outmigration, aging demographics, and climate impacts on fisheries and sea ice in Nunatsiavut, the Inuit-settled area of Labrador.
